questions.stem: A unit test asserts that two calls to Integer.valueOf(8443) return the same object. On the CI server it passes; on a developer's laptop, with the same JDK build and the same class files, it fails. What explains the difference?

options.text: The CI JVM is started with a larger cache bound, since the range valueOf shares is fixed when the JVM starts
options.says: the javadoc promises sharing only for -128 to 127; on HotSpot -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax raises the bound at start-up, so the same class files give different identities

options.text: The CI JVM has asked for 8443 earlier in the run, since valueOf keeps the values it hands out for later calls
options.says: valueOf shares a range fixed at start-up; it does not keep the values it was asked for

options.text: The laptop's JVM is short of heap, since valueOf drops its shared objects when memory runs low
options.says: the shared range is settled when the JVM starts, not by the heap later on; the javadoc promises -128 to 127 and leaves the rest open

options.text: The laptop's JVM is running interpreted, since valueOf shares objects only once the JIT has compiled it
options.says: the class files and the JIT are not what decides it: the same program gave false and true depending only on a start-up flag

origin.section: new Always Allocates; a Static Factory Can Hand Back an Object It Already Made

questions.stem: A Region enum has 60 constants, and forty places in a service build sets of it with EnumSet.noneOf(Region.class) and then add regions to them. A release adds ten more regions and the service is rebuilt with no other change. What happens at those forty places?

options.text: They stop compiling, since a set of the larger enum would still be one long, which holds 64 constants
options.says: the class is chosen from the enum at each call and callers only see EnumSet, so nothing in their source depends on the 64-bit class

options.text: They work as before, since a set of the larger enum is a different class that keeps an array of longs
options.says: noneOf picks RegularEnumSet (one long) for up to 64 constants and JumboEnumSet (a long[]) above, and callers only ever see EnumSet

options.text: They work as before, since a set of the larger enum is the same class, still keeping one long
options.says: one long holds 64 bits; above 64 constants the factory returns a different class that keeps a long[]

options.text: They stop compiling, since a set of the larger enum would need an array of longs, which noneOf can't return
options.says: noneOf returns JumboEnumSet, which keeps a long[], for an enum of more than 64 constants

origin.section: A Static Factory Picks the Class From Its Input, So the Class Can Change Without Callers Noticing

questions.stem: A pricing class declares double price = 1.005; two billing jobs convert it, one with new BigDecimal(price) and the other with BigDecimal.valueOf(price), and each writes the result's toString() to its invoice. What do the two invoices show?

options.text: The valueOf job shows 1.005 and the other a long expansion, since valueOf reads the double the way String.format("%.3f") prints it
options.says: valueOf rounds to no fixed number of places: it reads the double the way Double.toString prints it, the shortest decimal that reads back as the same double

options.text: Both jobs show 1.005, since each of the two calls reads the double the way Double.toString prints it
options.says: only valueOf goes through Double.toString; the constructor reads the exact binary value, which is not 1.005

options.text: The valueOf job shows 1.005 and the other a long expansion, since valueOf reads the double the way Double.toString prints it
options.says: the constructor takes the double's exact binary value, which is not 1.005, while valueOf goes through Double.toString, which prints the literal 1.005 back

options.text: Both jobs show 1.005, since each of the two calls reads the double the way String.format("%.3f") prints it
options.says: the constructor reads the exact binary value, as new BigDecimal(0.1) showed, not a rounded form

origin.section: A Constructor Can't Say How It Reads Its Arguments; a Factory's Name Can

questions.stem: AuditingExecutor extends ThreadPoolExecutor and overrides newTaskFor, so that cancelling any submitted task writes an audit record. A configuration class holds the pool in a field of type ExecutorService. A later change replaces new AuditingExecutor(8) there with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); the code that submits and cancels tasks is untouched. What happens to the audit records?

options.text: They are still written, since the virtual-thread executor's submit calls the newTaskFor that AuditingExecutor overrides
options.says: an override changes only objects of the subclass; the virtual-thread executor is another class and never calls it

options.text: They are still written, since the override replaced the Future class that ExecutorService.submit returns
options.says: the override returns its product only from AuditingExecutor's own submit; other executors build their own Futures

options.text: They are no longer written, since the new executor builds its Futures without calling that method
options.says: the hook reaches only objects built from the subclass, and ThreadPerTaskExecutor has no newTaskFor at all; the change compiles because the field is an ExecutorService

options.text: They are no longer written, since the new executor cancels a virtual thread's task without going through its Future
options.says: the caller cancels through the Future that submit returned, on every pool; what is missing is the override, which that executor never calls

origin.section: Each Product Costs a Subclass, and the Hook Reaches Only Objects Built From It
